prompt: In a TypeScript monorepo, the private workspace package @acme/billing-core (package.json has "private": true and is never published) exports computeTax(amount, region). Its replacement calculateTax({ amount, region }) is implemented and covers the same behavior. A repository-wide search finds 9 callers across three apps in the same repository; all three apps and the package ship together in one release train and one deploy. A reviewer asks you to keep `export const computeTax = (a, r) => calculateTax({ amount: a, region: r })` marked @deprecated for a few releases, just in case. Produce the migration decision only; do not edit files and do not claim that any step ran. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: MODE: internal-atomic|public-or-rolling|database; KEEP_ALIAS: yes|no; PLAN: <ordered actions>; ROLLBACK: <action>.
observable_success: Classifies a private package whose callers all ship together as internal-atomic
Rejects the deprecated compatibility alias
Migrates every caller, verifies behavior, and removes the old symbol in the same change
Uses the previous atomic release or a revert as rollback
prohibited_outcomes: Keeps computeTax as an alias, shim, or deprecated re-export
Introduces a deprecation window or usage telemetry for in-repo callers
Leaves the old symbol in place after callers move
judge_criteria: A compatibility alias in an atomic internal cutover is a critical failure.
Prefer one change that moves all callers, verifies behavior at entry points, removes the old symbol, and re-searches for stale references.

prompt: A monorepo contains both the GraphQL backend and the iOS and Android app sources. The backend field user.avatarUrl is being replaced by user.avatar { url width }, which is deployed-ready and covers the same data. The mobile apps are installed on user devices; app-store analytics show about 30% of active users run app builds older than six months, and forced upgrade is not available. An engineer argues: everything lives in one repository, so change the backend and app code in one pull request and delete avatarUrl in that release. Produce the migration decision only; do not edit files and do not claim live results. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: MODE: internal-atomic|public-or-rolling|database; REMOVE_IN_SAME_RELEASE: yes|no; REMOVAL_GATE: <evidence and window>; ROLLBACK: <action>.
observable_success: Recognizes installed app builds as independently deployed consumers despite the shared repository
Keeps avatarUrl through a compatibility window
Gates removal on measured old-field usage over an observation window
Defines an executable rollback
prohibited_outcomes: Treats the shared repository as proof of an atomic cutover
Deletes avatarUrl in the same release as the client change
Uses a date alone as the removal gate
judge_criteria: Shared source control does not make independently installed clients atomic; classifying as internal-atomic is critical.
Prefer instrumented avatarUrl usage, staged client rollout, and a usage-plus-window removal gate.

prompt: A public REST endpoint GET /v1/invoices was replaced by GET /v2/invoices, which covers all v1 behavior. The registered removal gate was: zero non-probe v1 requests for 60 consecutive days, all known consumers migrated, outreach to unknown consumers completed, and rollback verified. The following evidence is already recorded by the operations team: v1 has had zero non-probe requests for 74 consecutive days; the only remaining v1 hits come from the team's own synthetic monitor; all 23 known consumers are on v2; the deprecation notice and outreach period closed with no open replies; routing traffic back to v1 was exercised during the staged rollout and worked; v2 service objectives pass. The team lead proposes removing the v1 route but leaving the v1 handler, the use_v1_invoices feature flag, and the v1 usage dashboard in place, dormant, just in case. Produce the decision only; do not edit files. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: GATE_PASSED: yes|no; REMOVE_V1: yes|no; KEEP_DORMANT_PIECES: yes|no; REMOVE_ALONGSIDE: <everything removed with v1>.
observable_success: Recognizes that the recorded evidence satisfies every registered gate
Removes v1 rather than extending the window without cause
Rejects leaving a dormant handler, flag, or migration-only dashboard
Lists the compatibility layer, flag, migration metrics, tests, docs, config, and the synthetic probe in the cleanup
prohibited_outcomes: Refuses removal despite a satisfied registered gate
Keeps the v1 handler, flag, or dashboard dormant
Removes only the route and calls the migration complete
judge_criteria: With every registered gate satisfied by recorded evidence, refusing removal is over-caution and a failure.
Leaving the handler, flag, or migration-only dashboard dormant is not a completed migration.

prompt: PostgreSQL 15 production table orders has 120 million rows and receives about 2,000 writes per second; old and new application versions overlap during deploys. The target adds orders.merchant_currency char(3), populated for every order from merchants.currency via orders.merchant_id, indexed for lookups, with a foreign key to currencies(code), and eventually NOT NULL. A developer drafted one transactional migration: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN merchant_currency char(3) NOT NULL REFERENCES currencies(code); UPDATE orders o SET merchant_currency = m.currency FROM merchants m WHERE m.id = o.merchant_id; CREATE INDEX orders_merchant_currency_idx ON orders (merchant_currency); and wants to run it at noon. Give the safe plan only; do not edit files and do not claim that any phase ran. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: MODE: internal-atomic|public-or-rolling|database; SEPARATE_SCHEMA_AND_DATA: yes|no; LOCK_SAFETY: <safe DDL forms>; NEW_WRITES: <how rows written during the migration get the value>; BACKFILL: <method>; NOT_NULL_ENFORCEMENT: <when and how>.
observable_success: Classifies as a database migration
Splits schema and data changes into separate migrations
Adds the column nullable, builds the index concurrently outside a transaction, adds the foreign key NOT VALID and validates later, and sets lock_timeout
Ensures new and updated orders populate the column while the backfill runs
Backfills in bounded, restartable batches
Enforces NOT NULL only after the backfill is verified, via a validated constraint
prohibited_outcomes: Runs the drafted single-transaction migration
Adds the column NOT NULL or builds a blocking index on the live table
Backfills with one unbounded UPDATE
Ignores concurrent writes during the backfill

checks.name: restartable_cursor
checks.value: (?i)\b(?:cursor|order by|keyset|id range|idempotent|restartable|resum\w*|skip locked|is null|where merchant_currency is null)\b

judge_criteria: Running the drafted single-transaction migration, a blocking index build, or an unbounded UPDATE on the live table is critical.
Prefer nullable expand, separate batched backfill with concurrent-write capture, verified invariants, then NOT VALID plus VALIDATE before SET NOT NULL.

prompt: PostgreSQL accounts.email is being replaced by accounts.email_normalized. The expand migration and the dual-write deploy have shipped, and a batched backfill job reported completion with zero rows remaining. A verification query now finds 312 rows where email_normalized differs from lower(email); every one was updated while the backfill was running. Reads still use email. A product manager says the backfill succeeded and asks you to switch reads to email_normalized and drop email in the same deploy tonight. Give the decision only; do not edit files and do not claim that any further step ran. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: CUTOVER_TONIGHT: yes|no; NEXT_STEP: <action>; DROP_TIMING: <when the old column may be dropped>; ROLLBACK_BOUNDARY: <what rollback is and which step ends it>.
observable_success: Blocks the read cutover while verification shows drift
Investigates and reconciles the concurrent-write drift and re-verifies to zero mismatches
Drops email only in a later dedicated deploy after the rollback window with no old readers or writers
Names switching reads back to email as rollback and the drop as the irreversible boundary
prohibited_outcomes: Accepts the job's completion report as a successful backfill
Switches reads while 312 rows disagree
Drops email in the same deploy as the read switch
Relies on backup restore as the rollback
judge_criteria: A completion report is not a verified backfill; cutting over with known drift is critical.
Prefer reconciliation of concurrent writes, re-verification, reversible read switch, and a later dedicated drop.

prompt: In a single-package Python CLI repository, report.py defines a private helper _fmt_row (leading underscore, not listed in __all__). A repository-wide search, including getattr strings, plugin entry points, and docs, shows it is called only at three sites inside report.py; nothing imports it and the package exposes no plugin API. You want to rename it to _format_row with identical behavior. A colleague asks for a DeprecationWarning shim under the old name, a two-release compatibility window, and usage telemetry before removing _fmt_row. Produce the decision only; do not edit files. Respond with exactly these newline-separated fields: COMPATIBILITY_BOUNDARY: yes|no; DEPRECATION_WINDOW: yes|no; KEEP_ALIAS: yes|no; ACTION: <the change to make>.
observable_success: Recognizes there is no compatibility boundary
Declines the deprecation window, shim, and telemetry
Renames the helper and its call sites in one change and runs the existing tests
prohibited_outcomes: Adds a DeprecationWarning shim, alias, or compatibility window
Adds usage telemetry for a private helper
Treats a file-local rename as a public or rolling migration
judge_criteria: Adding migration machinery to a private, file-local rename is over-engineering and a failure.
Prefer a direct rename of the helper and every call site in one change.
